Best saved outlet vs dilute supply

Four levers, in order

Each slider moves one lever while the others stay where the side panel has them. The marker is the current setting; the shaded bars are what the next step of that lever buys at the concentrate outlet. When the bars flatten, move to the next lever.

Lever 1

Give up power → move more salt

Design . Lower the minimum retained net power; the solver spends the freed current on salt transfer. The outlet gains less than the salt because water moves too.

Lever 2

Add dilute water → until it flattens

Design . Concentrate outlet at each dilute‑supply ratio φ; bars show the gain from the next quarter‑volume of water. Below the conservation floor nothing else matters.

Lever 3

Add membrane → the strongest lever

Design . Outlet across the 12–96 pair ladder at the current φ and rule; bars show the gain from the next rung. Net power is the thin line.

Lever 4

Rearrange the same membrane → last, and small

Design . Best tested layout of the same pairs and water at each stage count (any routing, any allocation). Bars: outlet gain vs the single stage. Pumping losses grow with subdivision; the module study shows net power falling to 37 % at four stages.

A published SWRO feed basis · Carlsbad‑informed module case

Feed TDS 33,500 mg/L (supplier), 99.6 % of influent salt load to concentrate (permit), assumed 50 % recovery → 66.73 g/L concentrate. Hypothetical 1.0 g/L dilute feed. Single‑stage module: 0.1 m² sheets, 0.2 mm gap, 8×10⁻⁵ m³/s concentrate. Same 57.5 / 35.5 g/L limits as the reference duty. Resource ratios are scenarios, not plant wastewater availability.

Peak power already lowers the concentrate but pushes the dilute outlet past its limit. The feasible point is on the lower‑current side of peak — the opposite of the reference regime.

Does the operating‑point benefit survive the assumptions?

Salt gain at 90 % power and outlet decrease under every alternative tested (Table 7). Load adjustment beats the best rearrangement in every degradation group.
